en: Preface to the *Sūtra on the First Rare and Great Merit Spoken by the Buddha*, Inspired by a Dream of the Benevolent and Filial Empress Da Ming.
On the first day of the first month of spring in the thirty-first year of Hongwu, I burned incense and sat in stillness within my chamber, reading...
As I was concentrating my mind upon the ancient scriptures, suddenly a mass of purple-gold light gathered, filling the space all around.
In a state of daze, as if in a dream, I saw the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara manifest within the light.

His great compassionate form stood with his feet treading upon a thousand-petaled precious lotus flower, holding a rosary of seven jewels in his hand, walking before me. Unconsciously, I mounted a verdant...
Cloud-borne carriages were drawn forth; five-colored jeweled canopies, pearl banners, and precious standards were arrayed in profusion to welcome them.
They drifted and fluttered on, their destination unknown. After a short while, they arrived at a gate, lofty, spacious, and magnificent, unlike anything found in the human realm.

A golden plaque bore the inscription: "The Realm of Gṛdhrakūṭa. Upon entering the gate, a multitude of mountains surrounded them, their verdant hues concentrated like dark eyebrows, deep blue and azure.
The cliffs and red walls rise steeply and sharply; the crags and precipices are jagged, uneven, and towering.

A single stream winds and meanders around the foot of the mountain for over several dozen li along its curves. The stream’s flow is clear and limpid, a deep, cool azure in which even a hair can be seen.
There are jade-like blossoms, precious herbs, *zhi* and *lan* orchids, lotuses, peonies, peaches, and *tuhui* vines.
The beautiful spring holds its essence as radiance unfolds. As the path gradually reaches its end, one crosses a bridge paved with lapis lazuli, crystal, *carcāru*, and white jade.
There are several dozen rooms covering the bridge; its pillars are made of agalloch wood and its beams of sandalwood.
The colorful paintings are exceedingly magnificent. Inscribed upon it is the name: "The Bridge of Prajñā. Gold...

It was inscribed in large characters. The bridge spanned several tens of *zhang* in length, its height being proportionate to its size. After crossing the bridge, one travels along winding paths for several dozen *li*.
From afar, three peaks are seen standing tall and majestic, leaning toward one another as they reach toward the clouds and the sky.
The forests are lush and verdant, and mists and rosy clouds intermingle; pavilions and halls emerge faintly from the treetops. After traveling another few *li*, one encounters yet another gate.
Upon it were inscribed golden characters which read: "The First Seat of Enlightenment at Gṛdhrakūṭa.

Upon entering the gate, the paths were paved with lapis lazuli, gold, coral, agate, and various other precious gems. Clusters of bamboos and lush trees flourished there, their branches and leaves profuse and dense.
Graceful and flourishing, the lush foliage provided dense shade. Exotic flowers and rare blossoms were thick with vibrant beauty and elegant charm, their fragrances flowing forth in profusion.
Fine fruits and beautiful seeds, deep crimson, green, and purple, shone brilliantly as they hung downward. Peacocks, parrots, pheasants, and swans flew and danced, their calls resonating in harmony.
Furthermore, there were extraordinary birds whose voices produced sounds like the Brahma-voice, their pure melodies blending together along the path.
Beside it was a vast pond from which emerged five-colored, thousand-petaled lotuses as large as chariot wheels, their fragrance wafting intensely.
Beneath them, ducks, gulls, geese, widgeons, mandarin ducks, terns, egrets, cormorants, and kingfishers swam and soared about.
Gradually proceeding to the midpoint of the mountain, there was a group of women dressed in various colored silks and brocades, arranged in two rows; those in front held...

Behind the banners and standards, drums and wind instruments were arrayed; the music of the Dharma was performed in full, its harmonious tones resonating with a grand flourish. Blue lions and white elephants moved with dignified grace as they danced in formation.
Youthful attendants bearing incense and flowers circled about, offering their gifts upon golden platters and variegated baskets as they ascended to the mountain peak.
Avalokiteśvara led me upward to a seven-jeweled lotus pedestal. Upon the pedestal, the palace was majestic and lofty, with deep and extensive corridors and galleries.
Multi-storied towers and overlapping pavilions featured ten thousand doors and a thousand gates; gold and jade shone brilliantly, their colors vibrant and exquisite.

The eaves were carved and the gates embroidered, with pearl-arched lintels and lattice pillars. The jeweled windows were translucent and intricate, draped with shimmering nets of precious gems; the balustrades and column bases were all likewise adorned.

A multitude of jewels was spread about, adorned with various precious flowers in brilliant splendor. Necklaces, banners, and celestial standards were interspersed like the points of a compass, while heavenly blossoms, light and ethereal, fell and rose again.
Exquisite fragrances wafted and overflowed in rich abundance. The gathered radiance of the jewels blazed forth in a dazzling array of hundreds and thousands of colors;
gazing afar into the vast void, it appeared boundless and without end, while looking down, one felt as if soaring above.
Beholding the myriad mountains below, he gazed upon this sublime and wondrous sight and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence. He thought to himself, "My roots of virtue are meager;
by what accumulation of wholesome causes have I been able to reach this place? Avalokiteśvara smiled slightly and said, "This is the Bodhimaṇḍa where the Buddha preaches the Dharma.
Even after the passage of *koṭi* of *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* kalpas, none have been able to reach it, except for those who have attained realization."

Only those who have traversed the path of the Tathāgata may ascend here. Although the Empress and her consorts were endowed with supreme virtue and attained the realization of Bodhi early on, ascending to sublime and perfect enlightenment, they now face a great peril.
It is for their sake that I have specially come to guide them and deliver them from worldly toil.
The Tathāgata has often preached the *Sūtra of the Most Rare and Great Merit*, which stands as the crown of all sūtras; it is capable of extinguishing and averting [all calamities].
Amidst these manifold calamities, if one recites and upholds [this mantra] for one year with diligent and unwearied intent, one may attain the fruit of *srotāpanna*.
In two years, one attains the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*. In three years, one attains the fruit of *anāgāmin*. In four years, one attains the fruit of *arhat*.
In five years, one accomplishes the path of a bodhisattva. In six years, one attains the fruit of Buddhahood. The worldly people’s merit and virtue are shallow; thus, throughout kalpas...
"I have not heard of this before. The Empress, who is to become the mother of the world, possesses a profound vessel of merit and a perfectly luminous awakened nature;
she is most worthy of being entrusted with the task of rescuing sentient beings. She has now taken the nectar-water from a pure flask and sprinkled it upon my crown.
I feel only a refreshing coolness throughout my body and mind, and all my anxieties are stilled. My mindfulness is clear and lucid, with nothing forgotten. Thereupon, he emerged.
There was a scripture in one fascicle which he commanded me to recite from memory; it was the *Sūtra of the First Rare and Great Merit*.
After I had recited it once, I had a rough understanding of its great meaning; after a second recitation, I attained clear and thorough enlightenment;
and after a third, I could remember it without omission. Avalokiteśvara said, "Ten years hence we shall meet again. I still feel as though there is something more I must say.
I pricked up my ears to listen. Suddenly, hearing the voices of people within the palace, I was startled awake.
Both joyful and amazed, I sighed in awe and said, "How divine is this dream! I immediately took up brush and paper to record the sutras and mantras bestowed upon me.
He did not omit a single word. He only perceived a strange fragrance in his mouth, and within the inner chamber, a pervasive scent lingered for seven days without dispersing.
Heavenly flowers rained down from the sky for three days before ceasing. From that time on, he recited this sutra day and night without interruption.

In the autumn of the thirty-second year, Nan Guo led the Emperor’s troops to resist the enemy on the outskirts. The city was repeatedly subjected to peril and distress; however, I redoubled my recitation of this sutra and remained tranquil, free from fear.
The Emperor receives the favor and protection of Heaven and Earth, and is assisted by the spiritual deities; he bears the legacy of His Imperial Father,
the Great Ancestor, the August Emperor Taizu.

The late Empress Dowager Xiaoci has bestowed her profound virtue and great fortune as a protective shade. For thirty-five years, she has pacified calamities and established peace for the imperial house, presiding over the great mandate.
As I occupy the position of the Central Palace, I consider my own virtue to be meager and my abilities insufficient to assist her effectively.

Reflecting deeply upon the *Sūtra of the First Rare and Great Merit* preached by the Buddha as I was moved by a dream in days of yore, I find that every single word and phrase is endowed with the reality of principle.
Its profound meaning is subtle and inconceivable; indeed, for kalpas on end, no one has been able to hear it.
Out of compassion, the Buddha has brought about its salvation, revealing the secret cause that awaited its time. [The] Tripiṭaka... ten...
The profound words of the two vehicles are none other than means to enlighten the multitude of deluded beings and proclaim the True Teaching.

Now, fearing that I might keep them secret, I have had them carved into woodblocks for wide distribution, serving as a bridge for crossing the river of suffering and a shortcut on the path to awakening.
May they act as a vast and skillful means to benefit the world. Indeed, the Way is not distant from man; it is man who distances himself from the Way. For those with resolve...

For those who study the Buddha’s teachings, if they can truly reach the ultimate and wondrous purport herein, their minds will harmonize with the myriad dharmas and they will realize the True Vehicle.
They shall transcend Prajñā in a single kṣaṇa and attain Nirvāṇa in the snap of a finger; liberated from the mundane dust of the world, they will immediately ascend to Perfect Enlightenment.
I have briefly composed this preface to assist in its circulation, so as to manifest the wondrous Way for all eternity.
The First Fascicle of the Sūtra on the Most Rare and Great Meritorious Virtues Spoken by the Buddha,
as Revealed through a Dream of the Benevolent and Filial Empress of the Great Ming,
on the Eighth Day of the First Month in the First Year of Yongle.

Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was staying in the city of Śrāvastī at the Bodhimaṇḍa in the araṇya, together with a great assembly of one hundred thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. Their names were:
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva, and others; as well as eighteen thousand great bhikṣus, all of whom were...
There were untainted great arhats, headed by Ājñātakauṇḍinya, Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Subhūti, Ānanda, and others.
They had all assembled at the place where the Buddha was. At that time, they gathered various precious flowers and pure maṇi jewels for exquisite adornment;
banners made of the seven treasures radiated brilliant light, and there were many precious gems.

Lattices, fragrant flowers, and jeweled necklaces hung down all around. The palaces, towers, pavilions, steps, and windows were all adorned with exquisite jewels, their radiant brilliance shimmering and beautiful.
The Tathāgata sat in formal repose upon a lion throne of five-colored precious lotuses.

From the crowns [of their heads], they emitted subtle, wondrous light of a hundred jewels. This light shone brilliantly like lapis lazuli suspended against a radiant jewel-moon, possessing hundreds of thousands of millions of colors.
It flowed and poured over the crowns of the great bodhisattvas and arhats within the assembly.

The forest trees, flowers, and herbs reflected one another’s light; their jade branches and azure trunks bore golden blossoms and verdant leaves, spreading in lush, flourishing splendor. At that moment, ten...
The lands, as numerous as atoms, were all completely filled; they formed a single realm of the color of the seven treasures.

Those who had come from various other Buddha-fields all assembled at the place where the Buddha was. At that time, the great Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, sporting with immeasurable samādhis and supernatural powers, emitted various rays of light that drenched the crown of the Tathāgata’s head. All sentient beings, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic power, beheld [him] everywhere.

Throughout the entirety of space in the ten directions, Śāriputra then rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, bared his right shoulder, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One, throughout incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, my mind has attained purity and I have been born through transformation from the Buddha. He proclaimed—

By explaining the causes and conditions, one awakens to the limit of no-mind. I pray that for the sake of the assembly gathered at this supreme gathering, you will open the gate of skillful means and reveal the meaning of the foremost, most rare Dharma-seal.
How does one perceive the Tathāgata’s pure, wondrously pure, and luminous mind; the fundamentally wondrous, perfect, and luminous mind;
the jewel-like awareness, perfectly luminous, true, wondrous, and pure mind; the wondrously luminous, unsurpassed bodhi, pure, perfect, and true mind? What is it?
How can one perceive the Tathāgata’s subtle, wondrous, and luminous nature; his eternally abiding, immovable, and all-pervading nature of wondrous True Suchness (*tathatā*);
his nature of true essence, wondrous awakening, and luminosity; and his supreme *bodhi*, the wondrous, luminous, and pure nature? How is it that all phenomena are empty and non-dual?

How does one transcend worldly toil and depart from the signs of the mundane world? Furthermore, regarding the path of sublime practice for the unsurpassed vehicle and the various *samādhis*, how does one manifest the true and eternal, forever departing from all illusions?

We only pray that, out of compassion, you will bestow benefit upon us, extensively expound the profound meanings to awaken the multitude from their delusions, and cause all beings to be fully endowed with peace and happiness, so as to forever ensure the welfare of all sentient beings in future ages.
Those who have set out to seek the path of the Tathāgata do not fall into false views. Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground.
Thus he made his request three times, seeking to resolve his doubts. At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying: "Excellent, excellent, Śāriputra!
Now you, for the sake of the great assembly and for the sentient beings of future ages in the final period, deeply seek the Buddha-way. You all, listen attentively..."

"Listen attentively! All the assembly, having received the instruction, joined their palms and listened respectfully. The Buddha said: 'The people of the world cling to delusion and are bewildered by the truth; they are confused and inverted.

They sever and distance themselves from perfect illumination, remaining ultimately in ignorance. Looking east, they are confused about the west; observing south, they are dazzled by the north. There is nothing at all that is settled.
Only the self-nature of nature fails to see its own quiescence, not being free from false conceptualization. This is the primordial awakening of the source of awareness.'"
One perceives that which is perceived; remaining far removed from clarity, one fails to sever the delusions of ignorance and wisdom, giving rise to views of annihilation and permanence.
As various marks continue in succession, flowing and changing, they are drawn by conditions and views to form objective cogitation.

One sees before oneself empty flowers, floating clouds, the moon in water, dreams, illusions, mirages, and shadows—all these false imaginings and fabrications do not depart from one’s own mind. They entangle all who are deluded, like stirring up dust while seeking purity.
If one perceives only dust, how can purity arise? If one hollows out stone to make a boat, how can it cross the waters?
If one presses sand to extract oil, nothing will ever be obtained. The seed of True Suchness has been obscured by delusion since beginningless time; it is truly pitiable.
Now I shall reveal this to sentient beings so that they may perceive all that is real, remain far removed from false and inverted views, and attain ultimate purity.
Purity. If that is pure, then it is universally pure. Perfectly illuminating pure awakening forever severs ignorance.
It is empty of all marks and detached from all roots and measures. There are no false conditions, nor are there dreams, illusions, mirages, or shadows.

There is neither existence nor non-existence. One accords with pure awakening; space is eternally quiescent, without knowledge or vision of arising or ceasing. One should contemplate in this way; one should be without [conceptualization].
Wherever they dwell, they give rise to a pure mind; because they attain purity through seeing things as they truly are, this is called the first rarity.
The Buddha said: "If worldly people wish to recognize the Tathāgata’s mind-nature, know that this mind-nature is not possessed by me alone; all sentient beings possess it.
It is only because of the fundamental root of delusive conceptualization within their own minds that they falsely discriminate and become confused regarding the eternally abiding true mind."
One loses the nature of true emptiness and purity. Emptiness is like dust or floating bubbles; their arising and ceasing have no source.

It is like opening a crack in a dark room and seeing light; if one blocks that space with an object, what more can be seen? Since seeing depends on light, in darkness, what could possibly be seen? Thus, the various appearances of darkness can never truly obscure it.
When hearing a sound through a wall, there is hearing because there is a sound; if there is no sound, there is no hearing. This is not a case of "non-hearing."
The nature of sound consists of movement and stillness; hearing is neither existent nor non-existent. When there is no sound, hearing does not cease; when there is sound, it is not produced.
Even in a dream of pounding a drum, hearing remains constant and true. This is because the mind of the Tathāgata is known to be solely ever-abiding;

the nature of the Tathāgata is known to be solely unmoving. Apart from those external objects, the nature possesses discernment; this is the perception of the True Mind—the fundamentally wondrous, perfect, and original luminous mind.
The wondrous, wondrous, luminous mind is the source from which all phenomena arise; they are seen only by the mind. All that is spoken by the various minds is, in truth, not mind;

yet it is called "mind. To know that the mind is no-mind, and that in this no-mind there is no grasping—neither movement nor abiding, neither arising nor acting, neither "this" nor "that"—and that the mind has no boundaries and no perceivable location: this is the arrival at the Tathāgata’s nature, the wondrous awakening.
The clarity of fundamental enlightenment is wondrously clear; it clarifies non-clarity, and non-clarity is exhausted.

Because the principle of the root is quiescent and its definitive nature is such that manifestation and concealment are without marks, it is neither one nor different, neither discontinuous nor eternal, neither emerging nor entering, neither arising nor ceasing.

It is neither empty nor non-empty, and there is neither emptiness nor non-emptiness. This is because the nature of the mind is inherently luminous and the mind-nature is perfectly full; thus, through this luminosity, it gives rise to [all phenomena].

The nature of nature arises from false views; by means of the false, the true is manifested, yet the false and the true are identical to the false. If one clings to conceptions, then attachments and notions arise;
as the mind conditions itself and touches upon the false, the jewel-like awakened mind is extinguished. The true nature departs from emptiness and the nature of perfect luminosity is destroyed.

Various kinds of minds arise and various kinds of minds cease; various kinds of natures and consciousnesses arise and various kinds of natures are destroyed. The five aggregates and six sense bases are all void.
Delusion. The causes and conditions of combination should likewise be so. The seven great elements are perfectly interfused and fundamentally devoid of arising or ceasing;

they pervade the Dharma-realm and manifest according to the capacity of the cognizer. The self-nature of delusive thought arises from conditions; since delusion is fundamentally non-arising, there is no delusion to be extinguished.
By abandoning the deluded mind, the pure mind becomes clear and white. Contemplating the characteristics of the original nature, the principle is naturally fulfilled. Arising is due to delusion.

Where there is cessation, there is the arising of causes; where there is no arising, there is no cessation, and thus no cessation of cessation. When both arising and cessation are extinguished, the original birth is non-arising, and the mind is eternally empty and tranquil.
This emptiness and tranquility have no abiding place; this is precisely non-arising. It is free from the conditions of conjunction and disjunction.

The six sense-faculties are dissolved and the "one" is lost, such that awakened clarity is perfectly wondrous. You should know that such refined awareness and wondrous luminosity is neither caused nor conditioned.
It is conditioned; yet it is neither spontaneous nor non-spontaneous. It is neither non- [non-] nor is it neither-is-nor-is-not.
It is free from all marks, yet it is all dharmas, and yet it is not all dharmas. The Tathāgata is neither a dharma nor a non-dharma. All dharmas are empty; all natures and marks are empty.
This emptiness is without nature, neither defiled nor pure. All that is spoken of as the characteristics of dharmas is...
The characteristic of non-dharma is called the characteristic of dharma as it truly is. It is without inversion, immovable, non-retrogressive, and non-revolving.
Like space, its nature is non-existent; all paths of language are cut off; it is neither real nor unreal.
It is unarisen, unemerged, unoriginated, nameless, and signless. Having signs yet not being signs, it is truly non-existent. It is immeasurable and boundless.
Obstruction is non-obstruction. All obstructions are extinguished; that which is the extinction of non-obstruction transcends the realm of non-obstruction.

It is wishless, selfless, birthless, and non-dual. To be free from the marks of intrinsic nature is what is meant by non-grasping. By severing birth and extinction, one maintains true permanence. The constant light, fused and luminous, manifests ceaselessly before one.
Both the faculties and their objects, along with consciousness and the mind, dissolve away together. In profound stillness, the mechanisms of the senses are stilled.
Illusion has no intrinsic nature. How can one dwell in wondrous faith that is pure and true? With true faith, one attains clarity and mindfulness without omission.

Through the transformation of habitual tendencies, one practices pure and true diligence. When wisdom is refined and pure, how could there be deluded habits? Wisdom is luminous, tranquil, and profound; its wondrous essence is eternally concentrated.
By means of the light of meditative concentration, one enters deeply without regression. Interacting with the ten directions, one’s Way harmonizes with that of the Tathāgata. Awakening.

The clarity of opposites reflects wondrous images upon one another; once the light of the mind has attained eternal peace and sublime stillness, it naturally becomes unmoving, proceeding according to one's will.

By means of faith, one advances toward abiding, relying on practice to fulfill vows. Treading the path of the ten stages, one gradually progresses, transcending the stage of the ordinary person to enter the state of the sage, realizing equal and wondrous enlightenment.
This is not something obtained by oneself alone, but must necessarily rely upon cultivation; thus, the three practices are perfected and gradually [fulfilled].

Accomplishment is not instantaneous. By departing from desire and craving, one ceases discursive thought and does not disturb the fundamental mind. Because there is no discursive thought, the various consciousnesses become tranquil and still.

Abiding in this tranquility within emptiness, one immediately perceives the True Path. One becomes far removed from the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense bases (*āyatana*), as well as from that which is produced by the conjunction of causes and conditions, and from the delusions of arising, abiding, and ceasing, and all that is false. Proceeding directly with the mind alone, one observes [reality] from beginning to end.
Regarding the stages: entering the wondrous *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna*, reaching the noble path of self-realization, and gathering the mind—this is called precept (*śīla*).

Concentration arises from precept, and wisdom is triggered by concentration; this is the untainted (*anāsrava*). Thus, one attains the nature of quiescent permanence, becoming free from views of arising, abiding, and ceasing.
One then attains the supreme supramundane *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*. I now reveal this permanence to you all.
Abide in the nature of the mind. You all constantly see flowers bloom and grass sprout; you constantly see them wither and fall, only to bloom and sprout again.

That which withers and falls changes, while that which does not change remains. These various empty phenomena have no arising or ceasing. The awakened mind’s emptiness is indestructible and immovable.
The wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment is that upon which illusions depend for their arising. To seek awakening by relying on illusion is for awakening itself to become an illusion. How so?
Those who possess discernment have not yet departed from illusion. To say that discernment is non-discernment is identical to illusion. If all illusions are extinguished, this is called immovability.

One distances oneself from illusory objects and distances oneself from the mind that perceives illusion. When distancing itself is also distanced, even that distancing is discarded; thus there is nothing to be distanced. All illusions are forever eliminated;
the illusory body, the illusory mind, and the illusory sensory fields are extinguished together. Even the extinction of illusion is extinguished; it is not...
Illusion does not perish. Perfect Bodhi is the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing; the pure fundamental mind and original enlightenment are eternally abiding.
Pure and perfect awakening manifests as perfect clarity, like turbid silt settling until clear water shines through, or clouds parting and mist dispersing so that the blue sky reveals itself.
It is like a mirror from which impurities have been removed, its essence naturally perfect and luminous. All natures are without nature; because they are without nature...

Therefore, it is empty. Because it is empty, it is signless. Because it is signless, it is effortless. Because it is effortless, there is no seeking. Because there is no seeking, there is no aspiration.
One merely awakens to the fact that the manifestations of one’s own mind are mere conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) and thus does not give rise to them.

Beings abide in peace and happiness, firmly maintaining their prohibitions and precepts, and constantly embodying the equality of the Tathāgata. From the ultimate limit (*koṭi*), there is fundamentally no illusory mind; there are no names or signs. There is no...

There is arising and ceasing. One attains Bodhi, Nirvāṇa, True Suchness (*tathatā*), Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), the *amala*-consciousness, the empty Tathāgata-garbha, and the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*).
One shall then attain purity throughout the ten directions; until the end of the future, the nature of mind will shine universally.
Through non-dual quiescence, one achieves Unsurpassed Perfect Enlightenment. At that time, Śāriputra and the great assembly, having heard the Buddha’s awakening instruction, [were filled with joy].
Attaining what they had never experienced before, they were all filled with great joy and immediately spoke these verses in praise of the Buddha:
"O Wondrously Awakened, Immovable Tathāgata, Honored One! You awaken sentient beings and skillfully subdue them;
Throughout worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, you universally respond to offerings. Your wisdom is all-pervasive; you are the Truly All-Knowing One."
Though you have attained the three knowledges of the Three Vehicles, you are the Sun of a Thousand Rays, the One Endowed with Radiant Conduct,
and the One of Immeasurable Wisdom; you are called the Sugata, the Knower of the World, the One Who Has Transcended the World,
the Unsurpassed Being among all beings and dharmas, the Tamer of Men, and the One of Vast Compassion.
Following his teachings, he delivers the teachers of gods and humans;
the Buddha, the World-Honored One, the Bhagavān, whose ocean-like Dharma-sounds are distributed everywhere, is heard throughout the ten directions in a single kṣaṇa.
He vows to awaken the deluded masses through the True Dharma and forever sever all inverted conceptions.
"Permanently abiding, true, and not false—this is the wondrously luminous mind of pure nature.
Now I have attained perfect integration within this, transcending the ocean of quiescent extinction through a single gate.
The Buddha told Śāriputra: "This is called the first rare and great meritorious *sūtra* of definitive meaning."
In a past kalpa, I received the prediction of attaining Buddhahood from Dīpaṃkara Buddha.
If good sons or good daughters hear this supreme truth, which is no different from my own realization, they shall now achieve the perfectly integrated, pure, and precious awakening.
I shall now proclaim the boundless secret divine mantra.
Oṃ namo bhagavate pratyabhijñāya | oṃ nāthānātha viśa viśa | praveśaya praveśaya | namo bhagavate pradaradaradīradīradīradīradīradīradīra ||1||
Ti shu li ti wu shi li wu shi li bu yue bu yue svāhā | Oṃ namo bhagavatyai ārya-prajñāpāramitāyai tadyathā | oṃ dhīḥ śrīḥ śūre ti si me li ti ||
Buddhāya svāhā | Oṃ namo bhagavate sarvadharmagañjaprabhasattvadarśanatejorājāyārhate samyaksaṃbuddhāya ||
Dhṛtadanta-ta oṃ sustani sustani sarvabāhyasustani svasti svasti sarvakarmāvāraṇasvasti svāhā.
Oṃ amaraṇī-jvālāyai svāhā | Oṃ namo bhagavate ārya-pramitāśvārājñāya tathāgatāyārhate samyaksaṃbuddhāya arhadbhyaḥ | Svāhā.
Samyaksaṃbuddhāya dadyāt | Oṃ puni puni mahāpuni aparimita puni aparimitāyur-punyeśvara-nārāyaṇa-pratītyasamutpanna-sarvvasiddhakari-pariśuddha ||
